Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-15
Start: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Ravi Kumar (Clearsail VP Eng), Sara Lopez (Clearsail ML Eng), Derek Wu (Clearsail Infra)

Summary: quick status check on throughput optimizations for the POC. Reviewed last week's benchmark results, discussed continuous batching tuning, queueing behavior under burst traffic, and next steps for a longer benchmark run. Customer raised latency SLAs and encryption/audit questions.

Topics: batch sizes, concurrency targets, request queuing, KV/prefix cache hit rates, network latency, SOC2/KMS notes, next benchmark schedule.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining on a Thursday, appreciate it. Quick roll call?
[00:05] Ravi: This is Ravi, hi.
[00:07] Sara: Sara here.
[00:09] Derek: Derek.
[00:11] Maya: And Liam from our infra team, hi Liam.
[00:13] Liam: Hey all.
[00:20] Maya: Cool, agenda is simple — follow up on last week's microbenchmarks, look at continous batching effects, we promised a recommended config and a plan for the longer 2-hour run.
[00:28] Sara: We ran the 30 minute tests you sent, saw about 20% throughput increase with batching but p99 latency spiked when concurrency hit 64.
[00:35] Liam: Yeah that's consistent with what we saw — batching reduces avg tokens/sec cost but if the queue grows too long the tail latency goes up. Looks like the queueing parameter there was default 200ms flush, so messages waited a bit.
[00:45] Derek: On our side network is pretty stable, median RTT to region is 12ms but there are occasional 80ms spikes during peak hours. Wondering if that contributes to queueing.
[00:52] Maya: Good callout. For continuous batching we often tune two knobs: max batch size and max wait (time window). If you lower max wait to, say, 60ms, you trade a bit of throughput for better p99. Liam, do you want to share the config we tested?
[01:05] Liam: Sure. We tested: batch_size cap 512, max_wait 200ms, concurrency client-side 64. With that we saw token throughput up ~18% vs no batching, but p99 went from 220ms to 480ms for the end-to-end. When we reduced max_wait to 80ms and batch cap to 256, throughput dropped to +10% but p99 improved to ~260ms.
[01:23] Ravi: So that suggests an operational tradeoff — we can hit your cost targets with larger batches, but might violate our user-facing latency SLA of 300ms p99.
[01:30] Sara: Right, many of our flows are interactive, users expect snappy replies. Background tasks can tolerate higher tail.
[01:36] Maya: Exactly. We usually recommend tiering: route interactive traffic to lower-latency paths (smaller batches, reserved capacity if needed) and background scoring to aggressive batching. Also—prefix/KV caching can reduce tokens generated for repeated prefixes which helps throughput without impacting p99 as much.
[01:52] Derek: On KV caching — you mentioned some cache miss behaviour last time. Any metrics?
[01:56] Liam: From the logs in the POC we saw prefix cache hit-rate at ~38% for the sample workload. There's room to increase via prompt normalization and local client-side prefixing. Increasing hit-rate to 60% could drop total tokens by ~25%, effectively raising throughput.
[02:10] Ravi: Okay that seems optimistic but promising. What's the easiest path to test improvements?
[02:14] Maya: Two parallel things: Redwood provides a small client-side library to normalize prompts and an optional routing rule to pin interactive requests to a low-latency pool. We'll share configs. Liam will send the exact sample config.
[02:23] Liam: Also we can set concurrency targets on the Redwood side — e.g. limit to 32 concurrent inflight requests per model shard and rely on autoscaler to add capacity when queue length exceeds threshold. That smooths the queueing spikes.
[02:35] Sara: Autoscaler — is that part of Redwood Dedicated or also available on hosted?
[02:39] Liam: Both, but in Dedicated you have tighter control over instance-types and reserved capacity which makes p99 more predictable. Hosted has autoscaling too, but for strict SLAs dedicated is usually recommended.
[02:48] Derek: We're evaluating Dedicated since we have regulatory stuff. What about encryption at rest and KMS integration?
[02:53] Maya: We support KMS integrations for Private and Dedicated — we can provide the KMS integration notes and sample audit logs. We'll attach SOC2 summary docs as well.
[03:03] Ravi: Good. Also curious about cost math — if we pin a low-latency pool with smaller batches, how much overhead are we looking at?
[03:09] Liam: Rough numbers: smaller batch config (batch cap 64, max_wait 50ms) reduces throughput per GPU by ~35% vs aggressive batching, so cost per token goes up accordingly. But you can mitigate by routing only interactive traffic to low-latency pool and keep bulk scoring in aggressive pool.
[03:20] Sara: During the 30-minute run we saw queue depth spikes at minute 10 and 23 that coincided with a background job on our side — is there any way to priority-queue interactive requests?
[03:29] Liam: Yes, you can set request priorities. Redwood routing supports per-route priority and tokenizable quotas. We can add a rule so /chat interactive route gets higher priority than /batch-score.
[03:38] Derek: That would help. On the benchmarking front — for the 2-hour run, can you simulate mixed workloads (40% interactive 60% batch) and incorporate network jitter?
[03:46] Maya: Yes, Redwood can run a benchmark harness with mixed traffic and synthetic jitter. We'll include scenarios: typical hour, burst hour with 5x traffic, and degraded network with 80ms latency spikes.
[03:55] Ravi: Great. For the benchmarks, we want results on avg throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, cost per 1M tokens, and cache hit rates.
[04:03] Liam: We'll capture all those metrics and include token-level cost breakdown per route.
[04:07] Sara: One tangential question — function-calling and structured outputs add tokens due to extra framing; does that change batching behavior?
[04:13] Liam: It does. If you're doing structured function-calls often, you'll see variable output lengths which can increase latency variance. We typically recommend truncating optional metadata or compressing structured payloads, and for heavy function-calling workloads we tune max_generation_length and set per-route quantization profiles.
[04:27] Derek: About quantization — any risk to quality for our scoring models?
[04:30] Liam: For many transformer models we support 8-bit and some 4-bit quantization profiles. There's a small quality delta for sensitive generation tasks; for scoring/embeddings it's usually negligible. We'll suggest model-specific profiles after we see your eval set.
[04:41] Ravi: Sounds good. Back to today's immediate ask — Liam, can you propose concurrency targets (32/64/128) and expected throughput and latency for each?
[04:49] Liam: Yes — preliminary: concurrency 32 => expect 14k tokens/s per GPU, p99 ~250-300ms; concurrency 64 => 18k tokens/s, p99 ~350-500ms depending on max_wait; concurrency 128 => 21k tokens/s but p99 often >600ms unless you add shards or more GPUs. These numbers are noisy — we'll run the permutations in the 2-hour test.
[05:06] Sara: Can you include queue length thresholds for autoscaler to kick in? We want scale-up before p99 degrades.
[05:11] Liam: Recommend scale-up when avg queue time > 120ms or queue depth > 100 requests for >30s. Scale-down with hysteresis at queue depth < 20 for 2 mins. We'll include these suggestions in the config doc.
[05:23] Maya: Any blockers on your end to run the 2-hour benchmark?
[05:26] Derek: We need to set up VPC peering and provide a test IAM role for Redwood to run the harness. That will take a couple of days on our side.
[05:33] Ravi: Also want to confirm the data retention for logs — we need audit logs for 90 days.
[05:37] Maya: We can push audit logs to your S3 and retain per your policy; we'll send retention configuration steps.
[05:42] Sara: One more — can you produce a small cost sensitivity table showing cost per token vs batch size and concurrency? It helps our finance folks.
[05:48] Liam: Absolutely — we'll include cost sensitivity in the deliverable.
[05:51] Maya: Great. Let's recap action items. Liam: send batching + concurrency configs and cost sensitivity table. Maya: schedule the 2-hour run and share SOC2/KMS notes. Derek: enable peering and provide test creds. Everyone ok with those?
[06:04] Ravi: Yep.
[06:06] Sara: Fine.
[06:07] Derek: Yep, will do.
[06:09] Maya: Awesome. We'll target early next week to run the benchmark — aiming for 2026-04-20 for results. Thanks all, end of call.
